solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: British gong collected by US subject — that's tragic!

definitions.note: standing for the name of a Shakespeare tragedy

indicators.note: the gong is gathered up inside the subject, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: Americans call the school subject mathematics math, not maths
a CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour; 'gong' is slang for a medal

explanation.surface: An American pupil earns a British honour, and the clue exclaims at how sad that is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collected by' puts CBE inside MATH. 'tragic' stands for the title of the tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Scottish play is one of his great tragedies, so 'tragic' points to its title.

clue.text: Cross nurses flap, being volatile

indicators.note: the first piece holds the other like a nurse cradling a patient

parts.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey
a tab is a small flap

explanation.surface: A cranky nurse is flustered and unpredictable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like 'angry' but is the hybrid animal; 'nurses' means holds within.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mutable is changeable, as a volatile thing is.

clue.text: Vessel — one under a pint, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: a ship that trades along the shore
a beer mat set under a glass of beer

explanation.surface: A boat, or something measuring less than a pint of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one under a pint' suggests a smaller drink, but it is the mat that sits under the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A small trading ship hugs the coast, and a drinks mat protects a table from a glass.

clue.text: Royal composition is rot!

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, marks the Queen
an ode is a poem, a literary composition

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a royal piece of writing as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rot' looks like a noun (nonsense) but is the verb 'decay'.
explanation.definitionFit: To erode is to wear away gradually, as rot eats away at something.

clue.text: Writer requiring pen and good technique

parts.note: to hem in is to pen or confine
a way of doing something is a technique

explanation.surface: An author needs a pen and sound writing skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' looks like the writing tool but is the verb 'enclose'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist, a writer.

clue.text: Part of a plane that's mine put on tip

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece is placed onto the end of the other

parts.note: to cock is to tip or tilt something, as a hat
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Someone describes an aircraft part as a mine dumped on a rubbish tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip' looks like a noun (a dump) but is the verb 'tilt'; 'put on' means placed after, in an across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The pilot's compartment at the front of an aircraft is its cockpit.

clue.text: Measure once shortened, divided by two

indicators.note: the shortened word is split apart by the other piece set inside it

parts.note: cut means shortened
bi- is a prefix meaning two

explanation.surface: Arithmetic: a measurement is reduced, then halved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'divided by' looks like arithmetic but means split open by the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The cubit was an ancient unit of length, about a forearm's span, now out of use.

clue.text: One on the fiddle suits stringed instrument

parts.note: playing cards come in suits
a harp is a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: A fiddler plays something that suits a stringed instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the fiddle' means cheating, not playing a violin.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheat who swindles at card games is on the fiddle, i.e. dishonest.

clue.text: Entry document dismissed, as faint

parts.note: a pass is a document allowing entry
a batter dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: A visitor's pass is rejected and they feel faint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faint' is the verb 'swoon', not the adjective 'dim'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass out is to lose consciousness, to swoon.

clue.text: Little to savour, fed nothing, one could make breakfast

indicators.note: the nothing is fed into the sample, so goes inside it

parts.note: a taster is a small sample to try
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone given only a morsel, then nothing, still manages to cook breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed' puts O inside TASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen appliance for browning bread is used to prepare a morning meal.

clue.text: Genteel setting where Aussie boxer punches fellow combatants

indicators.note: the boxer punches its way into the team, ending up inside it

parts.note: people fighting on the same side make up a team
a kangaroo, or roo, is the Australian animal famed for boxing

explanation.surface: A boxing kangaroo lays into its own teammates in a refined setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'punches' means breaks into. Kangaroos are famous for boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea room is a refined, polite place for afternoon refreshments, a genteel venue.

clue.text: Graduate pocketing noble cut as cafe worker

indicators.note: the graduate holds the other piece inside like something in a pocket

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

indicators.note: the word for noble is clipped, losing its final letter

parts.note: an aristo is an aristocrat, a noble

explanation.surface: A graduate in a cafe job pockets money from a noble customer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' docks the last letter of the noble, leaving ARIST, which 'pocketing' places within the graduate.
explanation.definitionFit: A barista makes and serves coffee in a coffee bar, a job title for a cafe employee.

clue.text: Tree complete with pole, if not fencing?

indicators.note: the first word fences in, or encloses, the other pieces

parts.note: 'but' can mean 'if not', as in 'nothing but trouble'
utter means complete or absolute
N is the north pole

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether a tree is complete with a pole if it isn't fenced off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fencing' is a verb meaning enclosing, not the sport or a boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: The butternut is a North American walnut species, a kind of tree.

clue.text: Man down under put on game

definitions.meaning: in Australia a friendly form of address to a man, like 'mate'
to wear something showily, as a badge or a beard

explanation.surface: An Australian bloke is persuaded to join in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: Australians address a man as 'sport', to sport a thing is to wear it, and a sport is a game.
explanation.definitionFit: All three senses belong to one word: Aussie address for a man, to wear showily, and an athletic game.

clue.text: Where life is known to exist, it's terminal

definitions.text: Where life is known to exist
definitions.meaning: our planet, the only place living things have been found
an electrical ... connection is a terminal on a plug or device

explanation.surface: A gloomy remark that the only planet with life is doomed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terminal' looks like 'fatal', but it is the electrical sense: the earth pin or wire.
explanation.definitionFit: Our home planet is the only known abode of life, and the ground connection in a circuit is also called this.

clue.text: Office supporting uncrowned king in part of north London

indicators.note: in a down answer the office sits beneath and holds up the other piece
the king loses his top letter, as a head loses its crown

parts.note: Charles is the name of English kings
a den is a study or private office

explanation.surface: A government office propping up a would-be monarch somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncrowned' drops the top letter, C, from CHARLES; 'supporting' puts DEN beneath it. HARLESDEN is a district of north-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlesden is a district in north-west London, in the borough of Brent.

clue.text: Defined by layabout, earning big money for starters, online designer

indicators.note: the picked letters are bounded, or framed, by the layabout word

parts.note: a waster is an idle good-for-nothing

indicators.note: the opening letters of each of the three words are taken

explanation.surface: A lazy person who nonetheless earns big money designing websites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defined by' is read as bounded by; 'for starters' covers all three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A webmaster builds and maintains a website, so is an internet designer.

clue.text: Unadorned feature beneath a cloth canopy

indicators.note: in a down answer the feature comes below the letter A

parts.note: bald means plain or unadorned
the chin is a facial feature

explanation.surface: A plain detail is found under a cloth canopy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beneath' puts CHIN below A in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A baldachin is a ceremonial canopy of rich fabric over a throne or altar.

clue.text: Representation showing some light passing through door

indicators.note: the light goes into the doorway, so it sits within it

parts.note: a portal is a doorway or gate
a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A beam of light coming through a doorway, as in a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passing through' means sitting inside the doorway word.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrayal is a depiction of someone in art or acting, i.e. a representation.

clue.text: Friend, penning her vacuous article, succeeded in a few words

indicators.note: the friend writes around, or pens in, the other letters

parts.note: a pal is a friend

indicators.note: emptied of its middle, the word her keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A friend writes an empty article of hers that is briefly successful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacuous' empties 'her' to its outer letters; 'penning' means writing around them.
explanation.definitionFit: Phrasal describes something consisting of a phrase, a short group of words.

clue.text: Nonsense beginning in rough pub in the centre

indicators.note: only the first letter of rough is taken
the pub word goes inside the centre word

parts.note: a hub is the centre of activity
a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: Drunken nonsense starts in a rough pub in the town centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' belongs to 'beginning in'; the second is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, from actors murmuring the word to mimic crowd noise.

clue.text: Cupid links stroke with love

parts.note: on a golf course (links) a putt is a gentle stroke
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Cupid connects a caress with romantic love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'links' looks like a verb (connects) but is a golf course, giving a putt as the stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: A putto is a chubby winged boy in art, a cherub like Cupid.

clue.text: This water tester I'm disgusted one has broken

indicators.note: the pieces break into the toe, splitting it

parts.note: you dip a toe in to test the water
'ugh!' is an exclamation of disgust
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A disgusted person finds a water-testing device has been smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has broken' means splits open. 'This' refers to the puzzle itself, a Telegraph Toughie.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-reference: this very crossword is a Telegraph Toughie, so 'This' names the puzzle type.

clue.text: Touts unfortunately always hang around too long

indicators.note: an unfortunate turn of events leaves the letters of touts in disorder

parts.note: ay (also aye) is an old word for always

explanation.surface: Ticket touts unfortunately linger far too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges TOUTS to OUTST; add AY.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstay one's welcome is to remain longer than wanted.

clue.text: Course it's stuff and nonsense, ultimately

parts.note: to stuff an opponent is to beat them heavily, to rout them

indicators.note: the very last letter of the word nonsense is taken

explanation.surface: A grumble that a course of study is just stuff and nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuff and nonsense' looks like one phrase meaning rubbish; split it. 'ultimately' takes the last letter of 'nonsense'.
explanation.definitionFit: A route is a way or path taken, as a course is.

clue.text: I suspect it's designed to cover astronauts, primarily?

definitions.text: I suspect it's designed to cover astronauts, primarily?

indicators.note: letters designed are arranged by plan into a new shape
the word astronauts gives only its first letter

explanation.surface: A guess that some garment exists chiefly to clothe astronauts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed' rearranges I SUSPECT plus A, the first letter of 'astronauts' given by 'primarily'. Read whole, the clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pressurised suit worn in space is made to cover and protect astronauts.

clue.text: Old German instrument working

parts.note: a sax, short for saxophone, is an instrument
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: An old German musical instrument still in working order.
explanation.definitionFit: The Saxons were an ancient Germanic people, so one was a German of old.

clue.text: Apple tree surprisingly bearing first of apples!

indicators.note: the letters of tree turn up in a surprising new order
only the first letter of apples is taken

explanation.surface: An apple tree surprisingly bears its first apples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges TREE with A, the first letter of 'apples'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eater is a dessert apple, eaten raw rather than cooked.

clue.text: Synthetic fibre — the other clothes soft also

indicators.note: used as a verb: the outer piece clothes, or wraps around, the others

parts.note: 'the other' is British slang for sex
p (piano) is the musical marking for soft
'and' means also, in addition

explanation.surface: Racy talk of stretchy fabric, sex and soft clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' is a verb meaning wraps around. 'The other' is a coy British phrase for intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Spandex is an elastic man-made fibre used in sportswear, so a synthetic material.

clue.text: What one should do with a plan announced to get the axe

indicators.note: the words are spoken, and what is heard is a different word

parts.words: What one should do with a plan
parts.note: plans are hatched, so the advice is 'hatch it'

explanation.surface: Advice on carrying out a scheme ends with someone getting sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'announced' means 'hatch it' said out loud gives the word for a small axe. 'get the axe' looks like being fired.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchet is a small short-handled axe.

clue.text: Put pressure on to protect British nation

indicators.note: the phrase guards the abbreviation by surrounding it

parts.note: to lean on someone is to pressure them

explanation.surface: Pressure is applied to make one country shield Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to protect' puts B inside LEAN ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Lebanon is a country in the Middle East, a sovereign state.

clue.text: Training establishment sure to manage after cutback, investor finally being brought in

indicators.note: the investor's letter is brought inside the reversed pair
read as 'cut back': the pair of words is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: 'yes' is a sure answer, an agreement
to run something is to manage it

indicators.note: only the last letter of investor is used

explanation.surface: A training college sure to survive spending cuts once an investor comes on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutback' read as 'cut back' turns the pair round to NURSEY; 'finally' and 'being brought in' add the investor's last letter inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A nursery trains or rears young plants or children, an establishment for bringing them on.
